## Executive assessment

QakBot's 2020-2021 history is not a single breach with a single victim. It is a sequence of documented campaigns and technical investigations showing how a long-lived banking trojan also served as a mechanism for collecting correspondence, maintaining access and enabling subsequent attacks. Its changing delivery methods are important, but the more consequential development was the relationship between infected organizations and later victims: stolen business conversations could become material for another round of intrusion.

This study treats the malware, its distributors, its infrastructure and follow-on attackers as related but distinct subjects. A QakBot detection does not, by itself, identify a ransomware operator. Nor does removal of the original implant prove that every stolen message, credential or subsequent foothold has been neutralized. Those distinctions are supported by dated primary research rather than inferred from the malware's reputation.

The chronology begins with 2020 sample analysis, follows the summer distribution activity and autumn document changes, and ends with the richer modular picture documented in 2021. A short 2023 institutional afterword explains why infrastructure disruption should not be confused with complete victim remediation. The afterword is not used to insert later delivery methods into earlier incidents or to claim that the operation is currently eradicated.

## Research scope and how to read the findings

Primary sources underpin the study: original vendor investigations, response casework and a joint CISA/FBI advisory. Some describe a single sample; others describe a vendor's campaign visibility. None is a census of every QakBot infection. Source numbers refer to the reading register. An explicit reading scope accompanies longer documents so that selected passages are not presented as a cover-to-cover review.

The case distinguishes four kinds of evidence. A captured artifact can demonstrate what an examined sample contains. A controlled researcher observation can demonstrate behavior under the reported conditions. Response telemetry can connect behavior to an affected environment. A broader intelligence assessment can propose relationships among incidents. These categories reinforce one another, but they should not silently substitute for each other.

Historical disagreements about whether the family was first seen in 2007 or 2008 do not affect the central 2020-2021 findings. This article avoids resolving that discrepancy by guesswork. It also avoids treating an old product configuration or detection result as current guidance. The goal is to explain the observed evolution and its investigative consequences, not supply a deployment recipe or a present-day product comparison.

## June 2020: the captured document and the missing delivery evidence

FortiGuard Labs published its first part of a QBot investigation on June 11, 2020. It had captured a malicious Word document but explicitly did not know how that particular file had been delivered. The document encouraged content enablement while presenting a loading pretense. Its macro-driven sequence obtained an executable disguised by a PNG extension, with multiple candidate download locations. The examined payload used packing and checks associated with analysis environments. [1]

The source's admission about delivery is an important fact, not a minor omission. A researcher can understand the document thoroughly without possessing the email that carried it. Describing that sample as "probably delivered by phishing" is a hypothesis; describing a recovered phishing message would be a different evidentiary claim. This study retains that boundary instead of manufacturing a complete victim timeline.

The deceptive extension also needs careful explanation. The reported downloaded object was an executable using an image-like name. That is different from a genuine image that exploits an image parser, and different again from executable material extracted from a larger image container. The distinction matters because superficially similar filenames do not establish identical technical mechanisms across malware families or campaigns.

## July technical follow-up: collection and persistence in one examined variant

FortiGuard's July 8 follow-up described a core module operating within explorer.exe, persistent execution through registry and scheduled-task mechanisms, local-network propagation and collection of sensitive information. The research demonstrated capture of clipboard content and keystrokes and examined browser-related interception. Its analyzed configuration contained 150 command-and-control address-and-port pairs; this was a configuration finding, not a global count of active servers or infected organizations. [2]

The report is useful for showing why a banking-trojan label was incomplete even before the later campaigns. The same technical system could support several kinds of collection and continued access. It does not establish that every feature was activated successfully against every victim. An observed capability and a measured loss remain separate claims.

A response reconstruction based on this variant would therefore need more than a list of suspicious filenames. It would ask whether persistence actually existed, whether another process hosted the malicious component, whether local movement succeeded, and whether collected information left the machine. The research explains why those questions are relevant. It does not answer them for an organization whose systems were never part of the investigation.

## What the configuration count can and cannot tell us

The 150 address-and-port pairs in the examined configuration illustrate a recurring statistical trap. A list of potential communication destinations is not the same thing as 150 functioning controllers at the moment of an intrusion. Some entries could be unavailable, reused or relevant only under particular conditions. The article does not independently test those historical addresses, and there is no need to contact them to understand the distinction.

The useful inference is that the examined specimen had a set of alternatives rather than one hard-coded point of dependence. That supports an explanation of why blocking a single observed destination might not describe the complete historical communication capability. It does not support a claim that every alternative was reached, that every listed machine belonged to the criminals, or that the list represented the full infrastructure.

This is original analysis of the reported configuration evidence. In an audit, the stronger presentation would label separate columns for embedded candidates, observed connections and confirmed infrastructure roles. Combining those columns into a single "server count" would produce false precision. The same discipline becomes important later when comparing infrastructure disruption with host remediation.

## Response casework: personal email on a work computer

Kroll described an investigation in which suspicious messages from a subsidiary led to discovery of an employee's work computer being compromised after interaction with a malicious link in personal email. The malware collected thousands of messages and contacts across multiple users. Kroll's broader cases included locally stored messages more than three years old and collection artifacts that could later be deleted. Its observed cases did not provide evidence that attachments were included in the collected data. [3]

This account identifies a trust boundary that a simple "corporate email compromise" description would obscure. The entry interaction involved personal mail, while the information available on the machine extended into work correspondence. The distinction does not establish employee negligence or a particular policy violation. It establishes that the relevant attack surface was the working environment, not merely the nominal category of the inbox that delivered the lure.

The age of collected correspondence also changes the historical exposure question. A newly detected infection can involve old content. The date on a stolen message is not necessarily the intrusion date, and a malicious reply to an old conversation is not proof that the attacker has continuously occupied the sender's systems since the original exchange.

## The email-collection evidence had an expiration problem

Kroll's account makes clear why a later absence of a staging directory is a weak standalone conclusion. The collected messages and associated artifacts were not necessarily intended to remain on disk indefinitely. If a report depends only on a final disk snapshot, it may miss actions recorded earlier by endpoint or network telemetry. That is an analytical implication, not a claim that a particular unseen victim's logs contained proof of exfiltration.

A credible reconstruction would distinguish messages available locally from messages actually collected, and messages collected from messages demonstrably transferred. Where a collector's own log records a total, that total is a useful artifact but still needs interpretation. It is not automatically an independently verified count of unique people affected or attachments exposed.

The negative attachment finding is equally important. It should not be expanded into a promise that no QakBot variant could ever collect an attachment. Neither should a writer override it by declaring that all mailbox contents were stolen. The response casework supplies a bounded observation. Preserving that boundary is more valuable than making the incident sound complete when the available evidence is not.

## July 17: Emotet returned to observed email distribution

Proofpoint reported Emotet's return on July 17, 2020 after more than 160 days without observed email delivery. At publication it had seen nearly a quarter-million Emotet messages that day. It described Word-document attachments and links, and noted that Emotet had delivered third-party payloads including Qbot. These were observations of the Emotet distribution ecosystem, not a count of QakBot infections caused by that day's messages. [4]

The distinction between delivery volume and infection volume is indispensable. A message can be blocked, ignored, opened without execution or followed by a failed download. Even successful installation of one component does not prove successful installation of every possible later payload. Counting messages as compromised organizations would therefore collapse several different stages.

This milestone belongs in the QakBot chronology because it documents an important potential distribution relationship. It does not mean QakBot had been inactive throughout Emotet's observed hiatus, or that Emotet was its exclusive distributor. The chronology is strongest when it records what changed in one channel while leaving other channels open to their own evidence. It is not a single on/off switch for the whole malware family.

## August 28: a Qbot affiliate change in a larger campaign

Proofpoint's August 28 update described a change to a new Qbot affiliate in the summer Emotet activity it tracked. It reported more than seven million Emotet messages across roughly forty days, compared with more than six million over twenty days in the earlier January-February period. The update also described additional language and geographic targeting and Qbot's backdoor and information-stealing role. [5]

Those figures show why raw totals need their time windows. The larger summer total did not, by itself, mean a higher average daily rate than the shorter earlier period. More importantly for this study, both totals describe the observed Emotet mail stream. They should not appear in a chart titled "QakBot victims" or "successful ransomware attacks."

The affiliate wording also deserves restraint. It supports a change in the relationship observed by the researchers; it does not disclose a full criminal contract, identify every participant or prove that all distributors changed together. The historical significance lies in the service relationship: access delivery could be adjusted without requiring the writer to treat every component as the same malware or the same organizational entity.

## August 27 research: repeated development, not one definitive version

Check Point's August 27 investigation described a spring campaign, resumed activity during the summer and a series of version changes. Its sample table used executable compilation timestamps, which the researchers acknowledged could be manipulated. The analysis also described VBS delivery, padding, delayed execution and changes in analysis checks, including server-side decisions about providing modules. These findings were tied to the examined versions and the researcher's visibility. [6]

The version history supports sustained development, but its dates are not signed release records. A compilation timestamp can be useful when it agrees with other evidence; it cannot establish the first real-world infection date by itself. The same care applies to a researcher's explanation for a campaign pause. A plausible development interval is not a confirmed internal schedule unless independent evidence establishes it.

The server-side decision is particularly important for interpreting incomplete observation. What a sample does in one research environment may depend partly on what the remote service elects to send. Failure to observe a module in a particular test is therefore not necessarily proof that the operation lacked that module. It also is not proof that every suspected module was used in a victim environment.

## October 15: XLSB was an observed delivery change

Hornetsecurity recorded a QakBot campaign using Excel Binary Workbook files at approximately 12:40 UTC on October 15, 2020. Its analysis described a ZIP attachment delivered through a hijacked conversation, a workbook falsely presenting itself as protected by DocuSign, and Excel 4.0 macros that obtained the loader. It also reported poor static detection of the examined document and limitations in contemporary analysis tools. [7]

The timestamp is unusually useful because it anchors an observed campaign rather than a generalized claim about the entire year. It should not be presented as the moment XLSB became malicious or the first time any attacker used that format. The source documents a concrete combination of container, macro mechanism and social engineering in its visibility.

The detection result is equally bounded. A sample's result in a particular scan at a particular time is not a permanent score for every security product. Tools change, signatures change and behavioral analysis may differ from static scanning. The valuable historical point is that the attackers used a less commonly handled combination to complicate inspection. The article does not turn that finding into a current recommendation to trust or reject a product.

## The DocuSign pretext did not describe a DocuSign vulnerability

The workbook's claimed protection was part of the lure. In the reported chain, the requested user action enabled active document behavior. It was not evidence that DocuSign had encrypted the malicious workbook, that the service had been breached, or that a legitimate electronic-signature workflow required the action. This distinction keeps the case from falsely assigning the vulnerability to an impersonated brand.

The mechanism is best understood as a change in the meaning of a security prompt. The recipient is encouraged to interpret enabling content as the step that makes a document safely readable, when it is actually the step that permits additional behavior. That explanation is original analysis of the reported lure, not an assertion about the motives of every recipient who encountered it.

For teaching purposes, the useful comparison is between what the document asks the person to believe and what the observed sequence does. The case is not adequately explained by saying "the user clicked." It involves borrowed conversation context, a plausible business file, a familiar brand and a misleading explanation of the next action. Each element contributes to the trust decision without making the underlying file trustworthy.

## November 2020: election uncertainty became a delivery theme

Malwarebytes researchers reported a QBot spam wave using hijacked reply threads and ZIP attachments themed around alleged election interference. The contained spreadsheet imitated a protected DocuSign document and encouraged macro enablement. Their observed sequence downloaded the malware and described subsequent email collection feeding future spam. The theme was a criminal lure exploiting public uncertainty, not evidence that the alleged election-interference claims were true. [8]

This campaign is a useful counterexample to treating a topical subject as actor attribution. An email mentioning an election can carry financially motivated malware without demonstrating a state-directed influence operation. The report's evidence concerns the delivery mechanism and payload. A political interpretation would require additional evidence about operators and objectives that this source does not supply.

It also shows that changing the lure did not necessarily mean a new underlying capability. A previously observed interaction pattern could be repackaged around a current event. The investigative question is therefore not just what the subject line says, but whether the artifacts and observed behavior connect the message to an established chain. The article retains that technical link while rejecting unsupported political conclusions.

## The stolen-conversation loop

Across these cases, correspondence is more than a source of secrets. It can also be material for later impersonation. The original analytical model here separates acquisition of a message, construction of a malicious reply, delivery of that reply and any resulting infection. This prevents a common narrative shortcut in which the mere existence of a convincing reply is taken as proof that the apparent sender's account was actively controlled at that moment.

A copied conversation can preserve names, topics and contextual details even after the original host is cleaned. That does not prove every suspicious reply uses previously stolen material; it identifies one supported mechanism that a response team must consider. Message authenticity, sender-account state and endpoint state remain different investigative questions.

This model also explains why the impact may extend beyond the initial victim. An organization could become a source of credible-looking context used against a correspondent without its own staff intentionally sending the later message. The case does not justify blaming every apparent sender. It justifies examining headers, routing and the timing of the underlying correspondence before deciding whose systems were involved in which stage.

## 2021: modules broadened the post-infection choices

Trend Micro's technical brief described a transition from components embedded in the main executable to additional components downloaded after contact with command-and-control infrastructure. Its capability inventory included credential and cookie collection, email harvesting, proxy functions, lateral movement, hidden remote desktop access, Cobalt Strike and an Atera remote-management component. Its timeline placed discovery of the Atera component in October 2021. These were observed or assessed capabilities, not proof that every infection used the full inventory. [9]

The architecture matters because the initial file may not contain the whole eventual operation. A defender or historian who examines only the first-stage artifact could understate the available downstream activity. Conversely, listing every known module under one victim could overstate the actual event. The appropriate historical record connects each observed module or follow-on tool to the evidence for that engagement.

This is also why the term "loader" should not be interpreted as harmless or merely preliminary. Access that permits later tools to arrive can be consequential even before ransomware appears. The claim is not that ransomware is inevitable. It is that an investigation ending at the first payload may leave important questions about subsequent access unanswered.

## Trend Micro's geographic picture was telemetry, not a census

The Trend Micro brief presents a global activity view for March 25 through October 25, 2021. Its discussion identifies the United States, Japan and Germany as prominent countries in its monitoring and telecommunications, technology and education as prominent industries. The report also describes business and financial document themes during the first half of 2021. These are observations from its visibility, not universal rankings of all victim organizations. [9]

A country chart can easily look more definitive than its underlying measurement. To interpret it responsibly, the reader needs to know the observation period, the collection system and what a plotted event represents. A large number of detections is not necessarily a large number of unique organizations, and differences in customer deployment can affect visibility.

This study therefore uses the geographic findings qualitatively rather than inventing an infection rate or population denominator. It also does not infer that less visible countries were unaffected. The historical value is evidence of distribution across several regions and sectors within a specified collection window. That is enough to reject a narrow single-country narrative without pretending to possess a complete global impact calculation.

## December 9: a different trust surface in Craigslist relays

Microsoft's December 9, 2021 report examined three delivery patterns, including a campaign abusing Craigslist email relays. The attackers sent messages to harvested relay addresses, using an embedded image that impersonated a policy notice and instructed recipients to type a URL. Microsoft observed relatively low success in reaching the related domains and suggested that the added manual step contributed. The same report described modular infections and access being sold for later attacks. [10]

The relay example is not a claim that Craigslist itself installed malware on the recipient's computer. It shows how legitimate communication infrastructure can carry an attacker's content and lend it apparent credibility. The trust decision must therefore distinguish the service carrying a message from the origin and meaning of the instructions inside it.

The reported friction is also analytically useful. Social engineering does not always become more effective when it becomes more elaborate. A technique that complicates automated inspection may also ask more of the recipient and reduce completion. The source offers a measured observation and a likely explanation, not a controlled experiment proving a universal conversion rate. This article preserves that uncertainty instead of declaring the technique either foolproof or ineffective.

## A real process name did not establish benign activity

Microsoft's examined chains included process injection, scheduled persistence, credential and browser-data collection, and email staging followed by removal of staging artifacts. Its report specifically described legitimate process names being involved in malicious activity. These are findings about the observed chains, not a claim that ordinary use of those processes is suspicious by itself. [10]

The investigative implication is that the name of a signed executable answers only one part of the question. A reliable reconstruction also needs to consider its parentage, context, loaded content and resulting actions. The case does not support replacing a narrow signature with an equally indiscriminate rule that every instance of a common Windows program is malicious.

This is a recurring theme across the 2020 and 2021 evidence: the operation is carried by relationships among artifacts and events. A benign-looking file extension, an ordinary process name or a familiar email relay can be part of an attack without being intrinsically malicious in all circumstances. The historian's task is to explain the observed relationships, not turn each named component into a universal indicator.

## Ransomware follow-on was a possibility, not the definition of infection

The primary reports place QakBot within a broader ecosystem of subsequent access and ransomware. That relationship should change how an infection is scoped, but it should not erase QakBot's own collection and persistence activity. An organization can suffer a meaningful compromise without a ransom note ever appearing. Conversely, a later ransomware event requires its own evidence about how access progressed.

For this study, an analytical timeline has separate entries for QakBot execution, evidence of credential or email collection, any identified handoff or secondary tool, and any final disruptive payload. Empty entries remain unresolved rather than being filled from another incident. This produces a more useful account than writing a single arrow from "phishing" to "ransomware" and treating every intervening step as inevitable.

The approach also prevents double counting. A reported infected host, a ransomware-affected organization and a stolen mailbox can be overlapping measures of one incident rather than three separate victims. The sources reviewed do not provide enough consistent denominators to calculate an aggregate loss or infection-to-ransomware conversion rate for 2020-2021. No such number is claimed here.

## 2023 afterword: infrastructure disruption was not complete remediation

The August 30, 2023 CISA/FBI advisory described an August 25 coordinated operation that took over the botnet infrastructure and severed communications between victim computers and QakBot command-and-control servers. It expressly warned that the operation did not remediate other malware or ransomware previously installed on affected computers. This is a later institutional event, included to clarify the earlier ecosystem's consequences rather than extend every 2020 technical detail into 2023. [11]

The warning is especially revealing when read alongside the modular history. Stopping one control channel can be a substantial intervention without reversing every action that occurred through it. Previously copied correspondence does not return to exclusive control merely because a bot connection is severed. A distinct secondary foothold also requires its own assessment.

This article does not claim that the operation was unsuccessful, nor that it permanently eliminated every possible QakBot-related threat. It states the documented scope and limit. A successful infrastructure action and an unfinished victim investigation can coexist. The distinction is essential when evaluating a public takedown announcement without minimizing the achievement or overstating what it guarantees for individual organizations.

## Unresolved questions and excluded claims

The reviewed sources do not establish a complete victim count, a total financial loss, or the identities of every distributor and downstream operator. They do not demonstrate that every known module was present in each campaign. They do not support treating a vendor's detection ranking as a worldwide infection census. Nor do they establish a single original discovery year beyond the differing historical descriptions noted earlier.

Several tempting shortcuts have been deliberately excluded. The 2020 election lure is not political attribution. The DocuSign imitation is not evidence of a DocuSign breach. Emotet message totals are not QakBot infection totals. A historical compilation timestamp is not a verified deployment date. A 2023 disruption is not a certification that every earlier victim's credentials, correspondence and secondary infections were remediated.

These exclusions are not obstacles to a detailed case study. They are part of its value. The available evidence is rich enough to explain how delivery, collection and modular access developed. Filling the remaining gaps with familiar assumptions would make the narrative smoother while making its conclusions less dependable. Further detail should come from additional authorized evidence, not from borrowing facts from adjacent malware families.

## A case-specific evidence exercise

A fictional organization receives a convincing reply to a three-year-old email conversation. The message carries a workbook that claims content must be enabled to reveal a protected document. Participants first identify which facts are actually known: the visible conversation is familiar, the new message contains a file, and the file asks for an action. None alone establishes that the original sender currently controls the reply or that the file belongs to the named protection service.

The exercise then supplies synthetic endpoint events showing a document launch, a renamed payload and activity associated with a common Windows process. Participants must connect the events without deciding that every similar process in the organization is compromised. They also receive a partial collection log, requiring a distinction between locally available messages, staged messages and confirmed transfer.

Finally, a mock notification says a relevant botnet channel has been disrupted. The team explains which investigation questions remain open. The goal is not to execute malware or rehearse intrusion commands. It is to practice the evidence distinctions exposed by QakBot's history: conversation familiarity versus authenticity, delivery versus infection, capability versus activation, and infrastructure action versus complete remediation.

## Conclusion

QakBot's 2020-2021 evolution shows a mature operation adapting several parts of an intrusion workflow at once. The public record documents changes in document delivery and analysis resistance, the operational value of stolen correspondence, and a modular architecture that supported later access. These developments did not unfold as one uniform chain or under one universally identifiable actor.

The most defensible account follows the dated evidence and preserves its limits. It explains the captured sample without inventing the missing email, the campaign volume without inventing victim counts, and the follow-on risk without declaring ransomware inevitable. That approach makes the study useful beyond its historical period: it demonstrates how to evaluate a malware operation whose consequences extend beyond the first executable and whose most convincing disguise may be a conversation the victim genuinely remembers.

9. August 30, 2023. Summary and technical overview read; used only for the bounded afterword, not as a complete review of the full document.

Accessed 16 November 2026. No malware was executed, no criminal infrastructure contacted, and no stolen data acquired. Original analysis and the synthetic exercise are not additional victim findings. Historical product behavior is not a claim about current software defaults or detection coverage.
